'''Harold K. Lonsdale''' (January 19, 1932 – November 11, 2014) was an American scientist, businessman, and politician. A [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]], he ran for [[United States Senate]] in the U.S. state of [[Oregon]] three times, losing twice in the primaries and once as the Democratic candidate, losing in the [[1990 United States Senate election in Oregon|1990 general election]] to incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Mark Hatfield]]. In 2011 Lonsdale sponsored a research challenge to determine the [[origin of life on Earth]].

==Early life==
Lonsdale was born in [[Westfield, New Jersey]], the son of a Sicilian immigrant mother and a Welsh father who had been orphaned at age 2.<ref name=hamilton>{{cite news
|title=The Democrat is a green politician who faces a formidable task, but he says the time is ripe for an upset
|date=August 26, 1990
|last=Hamilton
|first=Don
|newspaper=[[The Oregonian]]
}}</ref><ref name=mapes>{{cite news
|title=The strong-willed Bend businessman makes a second bid for the U.S. Senate 
|date=April 19, 1992
|last=Mapes
|first=Jeff
|newspaper=[[The Oregonian]]
}}</ref> In 1953, he received a bachelor's degree in chemistry from [[Rutgers University]] and four years later received a Ph.D. in chemistry from [[Penn State University]].<ref name=mapes/> Lonsdale joined the [[United States Air Force]], where he once witnessed an [[nuclear weapons testing|above-ground nuclear test]], an event which he found thrilling, but also one which left him with strong anti-war feelings.<ref name=hamilton/>

==Business career==
Following his Air Force stint, he moved to [[San Diego, California]] to work for defense contractor [[General Atomics]] on [[artificial membrane|membrane research]].<ref name=mapes/> After General Atomics, Lonsdale was a scientist at [[Alza Corporation]] in [[Palo Alto, California]] for several years. By the mid 1970s, Lonsdale and his wife had grown weary of congestion and the lack of open space in California's [[Silicon Valley]]; on one occasion, his family moved a planned outdoor picnic to their kitchen after no suitable outdoor location could be found.<ref name=inc>{{cite journal
|url=http://www.inc.com/magazine/19840601/5296_pagen_8.html
|title=Life In The Silicon Rain Forest
|last=Benner
|first=Susan
|date=June 1, 1984
|accessdate=February 9, 2011
|journal=[[Inc. (magazine)|Inc.]]
}}</ref> Soon afterward, Lonsdale quit Alza and the family moved to [[Bend, Oregon]], where with his partner Richard Baker, he started Bend Research, Inc., a company focused on development of new technologies for industries such as the [[pharmaceutical industry]].<ref name=hamilton/><ref name=inc/> In 1989, [[Pfizer]] completed the purchase of a minority interest in the company, making Lonsdale a millionaire.<ref name=mapes/>

==Political career==
In the mid-1980s, Lonsdale became active in many business, environmental, and civic concerns, including the Native Forest Council.<ref name=mapes/> He joined the board of the [[Oregon Museum of Science and Industry]], headed a task force to have the planned [[Superconducting Super Collider]] built in Oregon, and was a co-chairman of Governor [[Neil Goldschmidt]]'s science council.<ref name=hamilton/><ref name=mapes/>

===1990 Senate election===
{{main|1990 United States Senate election in Oregon}}
In 1990, Lonsdale announced that he would challenge incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Senator [[Mark Hatfield]] for his seat in the U.S. Senate. Lonsdale's two main campaign themes were [[pro-choice|abortion rights]] (which Hatfield opposed) and [[Forestry|timber management]], in which Lonsdale opposed exporting timber from Oregon forests and wanted to restrict logging in old-growth forests.<ref name=attle>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_tY9AAAAIBAJ&sjid=dIYDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6996,626503|title=Lonsdale blast launches Senate campaign|newspaper=[[The Bulletin (Bend)|The Bulletin]]|last=Attle|first=Rick|date=March 5, 1990|accessdate=February 7, 2011}}</ref> Lonsdale also refused to take special-interest contributions in his campaign, instead financing the campaign himself.<ref name=attle/>

After winning the Democratic nomination, Lonsdale considered a longshot, began to close in on Hatfield as he attacked the Republican's record on abortion and the environment in numerous television ads. Hatfield, who had always relied on his stature as a statesman in campaigns, was forced to change his usual tactic of not engaging his opponent.<ref name=walth>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=PAIzAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ZusDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5596%2C4757872|title=Hatfield shifts gears in race|newspaper=[[The Register-Guard]]|date=October 21, 1990|accessdate=February 9, 2011|last=Walth|first=Brent}}</ref> Hatfield turned the environment issue against Lonsdale, accusing him of hypocrisy by presenting allegations that Lonsdale had allowed his company to dispose of toxic waste into the environment.<ref name=hazardous>{{cite news|title= Lonsdale Firm's Hazardous Waste Violated No Rules|work=[[The Register-Guard]]|last=Walth|first=Brent|date=March 21, 1992|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=6EJWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nOoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5442%2C4430859|accessdate=February 7, 2011}}</ref> The change of tactics stalled Lonsdale's momentum, and Hatfield would win the election handily, though this would be his last Senate campaign.<ref name=90gen>{{cite web|url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=3502|title=Oregon US Senate Race, Nov 6, 1990|publisher=ourcampaigns.com|accessdate=February 8, 2011}}</ref>

===1992 Senate election===
{{main|1992 United States Senate election in Oregon}}
In 1991, Lonsdale made plans for another Senate run at Oregon's other Senate seat, this one held by [[Bob Packwood]]. This time, he received a stronger challenge for the Democratic nomination, chiefly from U.S. Congressman [[Les AuCoin]], who resigned his seat in [[Oregon's 1st congressional district]] to run for the Senate.<ref name=mapes/> Lonsdale went after AuCoin, whom he accused of having been corrupted by [[Political action committee|PAC]] money over the years.<ref>{{cite news|title=The return of a career candidate|last=Duin|first=Steve|date=September 19, 1991|work=[[The Oregonian]]|pages=B07}}</ref><ref name=SeaTi51992>{{cite news|title=Great political lineup in Oregon primary, but it's not the NBA – is voters' mood a pregame show for Washington|first=Mark|last=Matassa|work=The Seattle Times|date=May 18, 1992}}</ref> Lonsdale also criticized AuCoin's ties to the timber industry.<ref>{{cite news|title=Demo Senate primary gets rough|first=Jeff|last=Mapes|date=February 9, 1992|work=[[The Oregonian]]}}</ref> AuCoin turned accusations of undue influence back on Lonsdale, pointing out that Bend Research had received millions in federal defense contracts,<ref>{{cite news|title= AuCoin takes Lonsdale's role in debate|first=Jeff|last=Mapes|date=March 29, 1992|work=The Oregonian}}</ref> and noted Lonsdale's reversal of support for nuclear power and belated opposition to the re-opening of [[Trojan Nuclear Power Plant]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Lonsdale, in about-face, opposes nuclear power, Trojan restart|first=Jeff|last=Mapes|date=January 5, 1992|work=The Oregonian}}</ref> Lonsdale received surprising support from Packwood, who believed AuCoin to be a stronger competitor, and ran television ads against AuCoin.<ref name=nyt92>{{cite news|title=The 1992 Campaign; Close Vote for Oregon Senate Seat Insures Recount|date=May 24, 1992|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/05/24/us/the-1992-campaign-close-vote-for-oregon-senate-seat-insures-recount.html|accessdate=October 8, 2009}}</ref>

The results of the Democratic primary were so close that an automatic recount was triggered.<ref name=nyt92/> On June 18, over a month after the primary election, AuCoin was certified as having won by 330 votes.<ref>{{cite news|title=State puts its seal on AuCoin's victory|work=The Oregonian|date=June 18, 1992|first=Jeff|last=Mapes}}</ref> Upon conceding the race, Lonsdale pondered mounting a write-in campaign, reiterating that Oregon needed an "outsider" in the Senate.<ref>{{cite news|title= A recount in the Democratic Senate primary is…|work=The Oregonian|date=June 9, 1992|first=Jeff|last=Mapes}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Lonsdale concedes primary loss with attack on AuCoin, Packwood|first=Jeff|last=Mapes|date=June 19, 1992|work=The Oregonian}}</ref> Lonsdale would receive fewer than 6,000 write-in votes in the general election, in which Packwood won re-election.<ref name=92gen>{{cite web|url=http://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=3501|title=Oregon US Senate Race, Nov 3, 1992|publisher=ourcampaigns.com|accessdate=February 7, 2010}}</ref>

===1996 Senate election===
{{main|1996 United States Senate election in Oregon}}
Following Hatfield's retirement from the Senate in 1996, Lonsdale ran again in the 1996 primary, but lost to [[Mentor Graphics]] founder [[Tom Bruggere]] by a wide margin.<ref>{{cite news|title=Smith, Brugger promise strong, positive fight|date=May 22, 1996|last=Hill|first=Gail Kinsey|author2=Bill Graves|newspaper=[[The Oregonian]]}}</ref>

===Other campaigns===
Lonsdale did not seek office again, though he sponsored several petitions related to campaign finance reform through the early 2000s.<ref>{{cite news|title=Initiatives would alter campaign finance laws|newspaper=[[The Oregonian]]|date=November 28, 2005|last=Hogan|first=Dave}}</ref> In 2006, one of his sponsored measures limiting campaign financing, [[Oregon Ballot Measures 46 and 47 (2006)|Measure 47]], passed, but did not go into effect because a companion measure ([[Oregon Ballot Measures 46 and 47 (2006)|Measure 46]]) that would have amended the [[Oregon Constitution]] to allow limitations on campaign financing failed to pass.<ref>{{cite news|title=Opinion: Get big money out of Oregon's politics|newspaper=[[The Oregonian]]|date=May 31, 1996|last=Lonsdale|first=Harry}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=32BWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=tfADAAAAIBAJ&pg=6254,2121215|title=Ethics overhaul moves forward in Salem|work=[[The Register-Guard]]|date=January 12, 2007|accessdate=February 9, 2011|last=Steves|first=David}}</ref>

==Scientific endeavors==
In 2011, Lonsdale, an avowed [[atheist]],<ref name=bhatta>{{cite web
 |title       = Scientist-Politician-Atheist Offers Own Money For Origin of Life Prize
 |url         = http://news.sciencemag.org/scienceinsider/2011/06/scientist-politician-atheist-off.html
 |last        = Bhattacharjee
 |first       = Yudhijit
 |publisher   = [[Science (magazine)|Science]]
 |date        = June 27, 2011
 |accessdate  = June 29, 2011
 |url-status     = dead
 |archiveurl  = https://web.archive.org/web/20110630220218/http://news.sciencemag.org/scienceinsider/2011/06/scientist-politician-atheist-off.html
 |archivedate = June 30, 2011
}}</ref> announced a $50,000 award to the best proposal that offered "a cogent hypothesis for how life first arose, including its plausible chemistry, and for how primitive life could have evolved to modern biological cells, including the present genetic material and metabolism."<ref name=bhatta/> The campaign received more than 70<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.originlife.org/|title=Origin of Life Research Award|accessdate=May 2, 2012}}</ref> and in June 2012 the prize was awarded to chemists [[John Sutherland (chemist)|John Sutherland]] and Matthew Powner.<ref name="www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk">{{Cite news|url=http://www2.mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk/john-sutherland-co-wins-the-origin-of-life-challenge/|title=John Sutherland co-wins the Origin of Life Challenge - MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology|date=2012-06-08|newspaper=MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology|language=en-GB|access-date=2016-11-18}}</ref>

==Personal==
Lonsdale married his high-school sweetheart Connie shortly after graduating from Rutgers.<ref name=mapes/> The couple had two children and divorced in 1985. He was briefly married to Portland attorney Susan Hammer in 1986.<ref name=mapes/> He married Bryn Hazell in 1993. He retired from Bend Research in 1994<ref name=vg>{{cite news
|title=1996 Voters' Guide: Senate Democrats
|date=May 19, 1996
|last=Hill
|first=Gail Kinsey
|newspaper=[[The Oregonian]]
}}</ref> and moved to Southern California,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.campaignmoney.com/political/contributions/harry-lonsdale.asp?cycle=12|title=Harry Lonsdale Political Contributions|accessdate=May 2, 2012}}</ref> where he died after suffering a [[heart attack]] in 2014.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.oregonlive.com/mapes/index.ssf/2014/11/harry_lonsdale_bend_entreprene.html|last=Mapes|first=Jeff|newspaper=The Oregonian|date=November 14, 2014|accessdate=November 14, 2014|title=Harry Lonsdale, Bend entrepreneur and Senate candidate, dies at 82}}</ref>
